title: Snatch
intro: Snatch asks what goodness is worth when obedience has not protected anyone. Its advice to start over becomes a demand to turn bad before injury turns a person inside out. The slaughtered, formerly obedient sheep supplies the grim example; the scam and false brotherhood make the grievance personal. Yet the song finally tries to recover hope, and admits that the voice offering it is unsure. The ending is neither a clean endorsement of cruelty nor a comfortable moral recovery. It is someone trying to imagine survival without another betrayal.
reading: Obedience fails as protection; hardening risks reproducing injury; tentative hope is a change in the speaker's certainty.

revisions.28-n1: The near-rhyme between becoming bad and becoming warped makes a cruel choice sound unavoidable. He argues that refusing to harden will not preserve innocence; it will allow injury to deform you instead. The obedient sheep then serves as evidence. This is the speaker's survival logic under pressure, not a general truth the annotation needs to endorse. Its bleakness is precisely why the final attempt at hope matters.
revisions.28-phrase-obedience: The sheep was well-behaved, and was slaughtered anyway. Approval did not buy protection. Its unresolved eyes and regrets extend the failure beyond the moment of death: even the promise of a peaceful ending is missing. The passage supplies the emotional argument for turning bad, replacing a vague tough-guy instruction with a specific fear of being valued only for one's compliance.
revisions.28-n5: Calling someone a brother is tested against whether they would share the consequences. The question is deliberately costly because names and professions of closeness have become cheap. At the same time, asking another person to take the blame is a demanding model of loyalty; the speaker's injury does not automatically make every condition he sets fair. The next admission of his own stubbornness leaves room for that difficulty.
revisions.editorial-28-owning: He accepts the charge of being stubborn and obsessively fixed rather than claiming complete innocence. That brief self-recognition distinguishes the voice from a purely righteous accuser. But it immediately gives way to declaring everyone an enemy. Awareness of his own tendency does not yet free him from it. The closing encouragement has to work against this narrowed world, not merely follow an uncomplicated list of villains.
revisions.editorial-28-hope-about-hope: The penultimate claim says the world still contains hope; the last line asks whether that claim is true. This is a real change from the opening's confident orders about what one must become. The person giving encouragement now reveals that they need to believe it too. The uncertainty here is the lyric's own emotional achievement, not an annotation's reluctance to take a position: hope survives as an effort shared with the listener.
